content: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory and support constant-time random access through an index.
A linked list stores nodes connected by references. Access requires traversal and does not provide direct indexing.
A stack removes the most recently inserted item first, following last in, first out.
A queue removes the earliest inserted item first, following first in, first out.
Binary search requires a sorted sequence because each comparison discards an ordered half of the search space.
Binary search repeatedly compares the target with the middle element of a sorted sequence.
Recursive call structure is commonly used to express depth-first traversal of trees.
Tree traversal visits nodes in a defined order such as preorder, inorder, postorder, or level order.
Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a queue.
Depth-first search follows one branch deeply before backtracking and typically uses recursion or a stack.
Appending to a dynamic array is amortized constant time because occasional resizing cost is spread across many appends.
Hash-table collisions can be handled with separate chaining or open addressing such as linear probing.
A weighted graph assigns a cost to each edge; shortest-path algorithms compare accumulated path costs.
Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths in a graph with non-negative edge weights using a priority queue.
